edits.old: The core question before the appellate courts was whether notice under Section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act (TPA) is necessary to determine a lease for non-payment of rent when the lease was executed prior to the TPA's commencement in 1882, and whether the High Court erred in refusing relief against forfeiture [S71cadf6075e5].
edits.new: The principal questions were whether notice under Section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act (TPA) is necessary for determining a lease for non-payment of rent where such lease was executed before the TPA came into force, and whether the High Court should have interfered with the discretion of the lower courts in refusing relief against forfeiture [S71cadf6075e5].

evidence.quote: The principal question arising for decision in the ap... peal is whether notice as contemplated by section III (g) of the Transfer of Property Act is necessary for the determination of a lease for non-payment of rent even where such lease was executed before the coming into force of the Transfer of Property Act . The only other question that falls for determination is whether the High Court should have interfered with the discretion of the lower courts in refusing relief against forfeiture in the circumstances of this case.

edits.reason: Corrects the phrasing to match the source's identification of two distinct questions: the necessity of notice for pre-TPA leases and the propriety of interfering with discretionary refusal of relief.

edits.old: In 1863, Ramabai granted a permanent lease of two inam lands (Pratibhandi Nos. 71 and 72, corresponding to current survey Nos. 86/1 and 86/2) to Ladha Ibrahim Sheth.
edits.new: In 1863, Ramabai granted a permanent lease of two inam lands, numbered Pratibhandi Nos. 71 and 72, to Ladha Ibrahim Sheth. Present survey Nos. 86/1 and 86/2 together correspond to old Pratibhandi No. 71 [S7d318e964c98].

evidence.quote: She owned two inam lands at Mundhava which were then numbered Pratibhandi Nos. 71 and 72. Present survey Nos. 86/1 and 86/2 together correspond to old Pratibhandi No. 71. On 1st July, 1863, Ramabai... passed a permanent lease of both these numbers to one Ladha Ibrahim Sheth.

edits.reason: Clarifies the mapping of survey numbers. The source states 86/1 and 86/2 correspond to Old 71. The draft previously implied a direct 1-to-1 or ambiguous correspondence with both old numbers.

edits.old: The Trial Court held that the lease terminated under Section 111(b) of the TPA (efflux of time/happening of event) rather than Section 111(g) (forfeiture), characterizing the default clause as one of nullity.
edits.new: The Trial Court held that the provision in the rent note regarding non-payment was a clause of nullity and not merely a clause of forfeiture; thus, the lease determined under Section 111(b) and no notice under Section 111(g) was necessary [S5afdea9718d2].

evidence.quote: the trial court expressed the view that the provision in the rent note that on non-payment of rent the rights of the tenant would come to an end was a clause of nullity and not merely a clause of forfeiture and that the lease was therefore determined under section 111 (b) and not under section III (g) of the Transfer of Property Act and that no notice as required by section 111 (g) was necessary for terminating the lease in suit.

edits.reason: More accurately reflects the trial court's reasoning that the specific nature of the clause (nullity vs forfeiture) dictated the statutory section applied (111(b) vs 111(g)).

edits.old: The District Judge affirmed the decree with modifications regarding the removal of buildings and trees. Legally, the District Judge diverged from the Trial Court, holding that the lease ended under Section 111(g) (forfeiture). However, it concluded that no notice was required because the lease predated the TPA. It upheld the refusal of relief against forfeiture [S6edc73b737af][S9e76c78f8751].
edits.new: Defendant No. 1 alone appealed to the District Judge, who confirmed the decree with modifications allowing the removal of buildings and trees within three months. The District Judge found the lease ended under Section 111(g) (forfeiture) but held no notice was necessary as the lease predated the TPA. It saw no valid reason to interfere with the trial judge's finding on relief against forfeiture [S6bd3b3405860][S6edc73b737af][S9e76c78f8751].

evidence.quote: Against the decision of the trial judge defendant No. I-alone filed an appeal to the District Judge of Poona. The lower appellate court confirmed the decree of the trial court with two modifications.

I was allowed to remove the buildings on survey No. 86/2 and also the trees therein within three months. On the issue whether a notice was necessary, the appellate court found that the lease came to an end not under section 111(b) but under section 111 (g) of the Transfer of Pro perty Act, but that no notice of forfeiture was necessary as the lease had been executed prior to the coming into force of the Transfer of Property Act .
The appellate court saw no valid reason for interfering with the finding of the trial judge on the question concerning relief against forfeiture.

edits.reason: Adds the detail that only Defendant No. 1 appealed and specifies the modification terms (three months) and the court's stance on interference with discretion.

edits.old: The High Court dismissed the second appeal. It held that the notice requirement in Section 111(g) was not based on principles of justice, equity, and good conscience applicable to pre-TPA leases. Furthermore, it declined to interfere with the lower courts' discretion in denying relief against forfeiture, noting that non-payment had become 'chronic' and equitable jurisdiction was not warranted [S718056c333a4][Sb9a6de106bd4][S2dfb023a47c0][Sc5fd4abc4b7b].
edits.new: The High Court dismissed the appeal. It held that the notice provision in Section 111(g) was not based upon any principle of justice, equity and good conscience. Regarding relief against forfeiture, it held the matter was one of discretion exercised against the appellant by lower courts, and unless satisfied that discretion was not judicially exercised, it would not interfere; it noted non-payment seemed chronic and was not a case for equitable jurisdiction [S718056c333a4][Sb9a6de106bd4][S2dfb023a47c0][Sc5fd4abc4b7b].

evidence.quote: that this provision in sub-section (g) of section III in regard to notice was not based upon any principle of justice, equity and good conscience.

On the question whether the tenant should have been given relief against forfeiture the High Court held that the matter was one of discretion and both the lower courts had exercised their discretion against the appellant and that being so, unless they were satisfied that the discretion was not judicially exercised or was exercised without proper materials they would not ordinarily interfere with it in second appeal.
become chronic and that this was not a case for the exercise of equitable jurisdiction.

edits.reason: Removes the inferred phrase 'applicable to pre-TPA leases' from the HC's holding on notice, sticking closer to the quoted text. Clarifies the standard for interfering with discretion.

edits.anchor: The Supreme Court appeal focuses on survey No. 86/2.
edits.new: The appeal is confined to survey No. 86/2 at Mundhava in Poona district [S7a87f7dac1cd].

evidence.quote: The appeal is confined to survey No. 86/2 at Mundhava in Poona district.

edits.reason: Explicitly states the confinement of the appeal to Survey No. 86/2, which is crucial for distinguishing the scope of the litigation from the original lease of two lands.

unresolved: The draft mentions 'estoppel and waiver under Sections 112 and 115 of the Evidence Act' in the final paragraph. While S3516027004fb, S023f57fe0bc0, and S7e60a543f230 describe factual waivers (acceptance of rent), the provided sources do not contain the lower courts' explicit legal reasoning invoking Section 115 of the Evidence Act or Section 112 of the TPA to deny relief in the *present* suit. The denial of relief was based on 'contumacious conduct' and 'chronic' default (S006dde7cf872, Sc5fd4abc4b7b). The link to Estoppel/Waiver statutes is an analytical addition not directly supported by the quoted findings of the courts in the provided excerpts.
